## Today we cover

::: {.incremental}
- what "next generation" actually means — and the **three generations**;
- **second generation**: 454, SOLiD, Illumina, MGI — and the workflow they share;
- **third generation**: HeliScope, PacBio, nanopore — single molecules, long reads;
- **methodological advances**: hybrid assembly, targeted and deep sequencing;
- **molecular ecology applications**: markers, SNPs, transcriptomics, epigenomics.
:::

## Next-generation sequencing (NGS)

::: {.incremental}
- **First generation** — Sanger's dideoxynucleotide chain-termination method (**1977**); low throughput.
- **Second generation** — high throughput, **requires amplification**, massively parallel sequencing (MPS).
- **Third generation** — high throughput, **no amplification required**, single-molecule platforms.
:::

![](/assets/lecture3/p03_2.jpg){height="230px"}

## Some terms

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- **Read length**; sequence reads and **Gbp** obtained per run;
- **amplicon** sequencing vs **shotgun** sequencing;
- **base call**, **depth of coverage**, average read depth;
- **Phred quality score (Q)** — assigned to every base call;
- **FASTA vs FASTQ** — FASTQ encodes Q scores alongside the read.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p04_3.jpg)
:::
:::

## Phred scores are logarithmic

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p04_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r phred, echo=TRUE}
tibble::tibble(Q = c(10, 20, 30, 40)) |>
  mutate(p_error  = 10^(-Q/10),
         accuracy = scales::percent(1 - p_error,
                                    accuracy = 0.0001)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**Q30** — the usual quality threshold — means one wrong base in a thousand. At 300 bp per read that is still, on average, **0.3 errors per read**.
:::
:::

## Multiplexing

![](/assets/lecture3/p05_2.jpg)

Multiplexing lets a large number of libraries be **pooled and sequenced together** in a single run. Each library carries an index (barcode); after sequencing, reads are **demultiplexed** back to their sample and aligned.

::: {.notes}
Index hopping is the failure mode: reads assigned to the wrong sample. It is why dual unique indexes became standard.
:::

# Second generation

## The workflow they all share

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p06_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p20_2.jpg)
:::
:::

Fragment → adapters → **clonal amplification** → immobilise on a surface → cycle chemistry with imaging → base calls → assembly or mapping.

## Pyrosequencing — Roche 454

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p07_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- The **first** commercial next-generation platform: Roche 454 **GenomeSequencer (2005)**; the technology existed from the mid-1990s.
- **Sequencing by synthesis**:
  1. ligate 454-specific adapters to fragments;
  2. bind **one fragment per bead**;
  3. **emulsion PCR** (emPCR);
  4. load beads into the **picotiter plate**.
:::
:::

## Pyrosequencing — the chemistry

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p08_2.jpg)

![](/assets/lecture3/p08_4.jpg){height="150px"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p08_3.jpg){height="300px"}

Cycles of dTTP, dCTP, dGTP — but **dATPαS** instead of dATP, because luciferase would use ATP itself.

**PPi** released on incorporation → **APS** → ATP → luciferase → **light**, read by a CCD camera. **Apyrase** degrades unincorporated nucleotides between cycles.
:::
:::

## Pyrosequencing — why it died

::: {.incremental}
- **Disadvantages**: high sequence error rate — especially in **homopolymers**, where light intensity has to be read as a length — and comparatively few reads per run.
- Early landmark use: one million base pairs of **Neanderthal DNA** (Green *et al.* 2006).
- Roche announced **discontinuation in 2013**, and stopped supporting the platform entirely during **2016**.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
454 gave 16S researchers their first community-scale datasets. A great deal of early microbial-ecology literature carries its homopolymer errors as OTU inflation.
:::

## SOLiD

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p10_2.jpg){height="70px"}

![](/assets/lecture3/p10_3.jpg)

![](/assets/lecture3/p10_4.jpg)

![](/assets/lecture3/p10_5.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Introduced in **autumn 2007**.
- Parallel sequencing by stepwise **ligation** — *sequencing by ligation*, not synthesis.
- Extremely high throughput of **short reads**, cheaply.
- Like 454: **emPCR** — but the beads are then covalently attached to a **glass slide**.
:::
:::

## SOLiD — two-base encoding

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p11_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
Fluorescent-labelled DNA **octamers**, a **di-base colour code**, and **five universal sequencing primers** offset by one position.

Every base is interrogated **twice**, in two different ligation rounds — which is what gave SOLiD its inherent error correction.
:::
:::

## Illumina (Solexa)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p12_2.jpg)

![](/assets/lecture3/p12_3.jpg){height="90px"}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- **1998** — Solexa founded by Cambridge-based researchers;
- **2004** — Solexa acquires molecular clustering technology from Manteia;
- **2006** — Genome Analyzer, the first Solexa sequencer;
- **2007** — Illumina acquires Solexa.

Cheaper to produce and more competitively priced than 454.

**Cost of a human genome:** $10M in 2007 → $100k in 2009 → **$1000 in 2014**.
:::
:::

## Illumina — library and cluster generation

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p13_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Sequencing by synthesis**, on a flow cell:

- a system of adapters and complementary adapters (**tagmentation**);
- **cluster generation** on the chip via **bridge amplification**;
- annealing of the sequencing primer.

Each cluster is ~1000 identical copies — enough photons to see one base.
:::
:::

## Illumina — the cycle

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p14_2.jpg)

![](/assets/lecture3/p14_5.jpg){height="170px"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p14_3.jpg)

**Reversible terminators** carry a dye and a 3′ blocking group. Extend one base, image, cleave the dye and the block, repeat.

**4-channel** systems use four dyes; **2-channel** systems encode the four bases as red, green, both, or neither.
:::
:::

## Illumina — from image to file

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p15_2.jpg){height="400px"}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p14_4.jpg)

Several million clusters are amplified at distinguishable locations, imaged by camera, and turned into per-cluster base calls in a text file.
:::
:::

## Single-end and paired-end

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p16_2.jpg)

![](/assets/lecture3/p16_3.jpg){height="200px"}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- **Single-end (SE)** — one read from one end of the insert.
- **Paired-end (PE)** — a second read from the other end. Reads 1 and 2 must **overlap** if you want the full insert sequence.

The **insert size** and the **inner distance** are the numbers your assembler and your amplicon merger both need.
:::
:::

## MGI — a second-generation alternative

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p17_2.jpg)

![](/assets/lecture3/p18_2.jpg){height="200px"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p17_4.jpg){height="90px"}

Library preparation ends in **circularisation**: the insert plus barcode is closed into a single-stranded circle with a splint oligo.
:::
:::

## MGI — DNA nanoballs

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p18_3.jpg)

- linear amplification
- always from the **original template**
- low amplification bias
- **no error accumulation**
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p17_3.jpg){height="220px"}

**Rolling circle amplification** copies the circle hundreds of times into one long concatemer that folds into a **DNA nanoball** — many copies, one molecule of origin.
:::
:::

## MGI — flow cell and chemistry

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p19_2.jpg)

![](/assets/lecture3/p19_3.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p19_5.jpg)

Nanoballs are loaded onto a **patterned array flow cell** — one ball per spot, by electrostatic interaction — and read by **cPAS** (combinatorial probe anchor synthesis).
:::
:::

# Third generation

## HeliScope

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p23_2.jpg){height="380px"}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p23_3.jpg){height="230px"}

The Helicos single-molecule device:

- **no clonal amplification**;
- a highly sensitive fluorescence detection system;
- sequencing by synthesis, with fragments hybridised to primers anchored at **random positions** on a glass cover slip.
:::
:::

## PacBio

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p24_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p24_3.jpg){height="80px"}

**2010 — Pacific Biosciences real-time sequencing.** A single polymerase sits at the bottom of a zero-mode waveguide; phospholinked nucleotides fluoresce as they are incorporated, and the pulse pattern *is* the sequence.

Because the same circular template is read repeatedly, random error averages out — the basis of HiFi reads.
:::
:::

## ZS Genetics

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p25_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
The ZSG process lets **electron microscopes "see" DNA**, labelled with unique contrast-atom labels.

- automated imaging;
- **5,000–7,000 bp** per molecule;
- built-in error checking by comparing information from the **two strands**.
:::
:::

## Nanopore technology

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p26_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- **Oxford Nanopore Technologies**;
- **MinION**: about 500 tiny pores on a flow cell;
- small and cheap;
- high error rate;
- **long reads**.

Biological nanopores for DNA sequencing were first proposed in the **1990s** and made commercially available in **May 2014**.
:::
:::

## MinION

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p27_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
The first commercial nanopore sequencing device:

- high-throughput sequencing apparatus;
- produces **real-time** data;
- inexpensive;
- pocket-sized and **portable**.

::: {.callout-tip}
Portability changes study design, not just logistics: sequencing at the sampling site removes the cold chain and the shipping permit from the critical path.
:::
:::
:::

## How nanopore sequencing works

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p29_1.jpg){height="400px"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
1. One protein **unzips** the double helix into two strands.
2. A second protein forms the **pore** in the membrane and holds an *adapter* molecule.
3. Negatively charged DNA travels through the channel towards the **positive** charge, changing the membrane's electrical conductance.
4. Current alternations, in the range of **picoamperes**, are characteristic of the bases in the pore.
:::
:::

## Reading the current

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p28_2.jpg){height="400px"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p29_2.jpg){height="400px"}
:::
:::

The signal is not one base at a time — several bases sit in the constriction together, so basecalling is a model over a **k-mer** of current levels.

## Nanopore data processing

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p30_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
1. **Segmentation** of the raw current squiggle;
2. **base calling** — increasingly a neural network;
3. **alignment** to a genome.

Because basecalling is a model, old data can be recalled with a better model years later.
:::
:::

## Devices and flow cells

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p31_1.jpg)

Flongle · MinION · SmidgION · GridION · PromethION
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p31_2.jpg){height="230px"}

Pore chemistry matters as much as the device: **R9.4.1** reads through a single constriction, **R10** through two — better homopolymer accuracy.
:::
:::

## Flow cell basics

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p32_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p32_2.jpg)

Three compartments — common reservoir, bulk buffer, buffer in the wells — shipped with storage buffer in all three, so the running buffer can be changed without changing the electrochemistry.
:::
:::

## Comparison

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
| Technology | Reads per run | Read length |
|---|---:|---:|
| Sanger (96-well plate) | 96 | 1,000 |
| Roche 454 (FLX) | 700k | 700 |
| SOLiD (5500 W) | 266M | 100 |
| Illumina (HiSeq) | 312M | 300 |
| PacBio (Sequel) | 370k | 20,000 |
| Nanopore (MinION) | 2M | 1,000–100,000 |
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r platform-plot, fig.height=4.2}
ggplot(platforms, aes(read_length, reads_per_run, colour = generation)) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = platform), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "read length (bases, log)", y = "reads per run (log)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Nobody is best at both axes — which is the whole argument for hybrid approaches.
:::
:::

# Methodological advances

## Platforms side by side

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p35_2.jpg){height="400px"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p35_3.jpg){height="400px"}

Human Genome Project · second generation · third generation — the same problem, three amounts of cloning.
:::
:::

## Combining short and long reads

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p36_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
Combining the strengths of different technologies:

- **short**, but low error rate;
- **long**, but high error rate.

Used for **de novo genome assembly** and for **(meta)transcriptomics**, where long reads resolve isoforms that short reads only imply.
:::
:::

## A real hybrid workflow

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p37_2.jpg){height="180px"}

15 *Escherichia coli* and 10 *Staphylococcus aureus* isolates from livestock and food; GeneJET genomic DNA purification.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p37_6.jpg){height="90px"}

**Short reads** — NextSeq (Illumina), paired-end 2 × 150 bp, 1.9–9.1 M reads per genome, Q > 20, fastp for QC and adapter removal, SPAdes de novo assembly.

![](/assets/lecture3/p37_5.jpg){height="90px"}

**Long reads** — up to 269 kbp, combined with the short-read assembly.
:::
:::

## Targeted sequencing

::: {.incremental}
- **Targeted sequencing (TS)** — sequencing only a subset of genes or genomic regions.
- **Target enrichment** — capture of regions of interest, e.g. hybridisation to **biotinylated probes** isolated by magnetic pull-down.
- Fewer targets means **much higher coverage**, and so more information per sample for population analyses.
- Sequence capture: **NimbleGen** (Roche), **SureSelect** (Agilent); **RainStorm** (up to 4000 primer pairs); **amplicon sequencing**.
:::

![](/assets/lecture3/p39_3.jpg){height="180px"}

## Exome sequencing

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p39_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- **Exome sequencing**, using exon capture, is one of the most widely used targeted methods.
- The **exome** is the part of the genome formed by exons — the protein-encoding part of genes.
- It usually represents **less than 2%** of most eukaryotic genomes.
:::
:::

## Adaptive sequencing (ONT)

![](/assets/lecture3/p40_2.jpg)

The pore reads the first part of a molecule, the software decides whether it is **in the region of interest**, and if not the voltage is reversed to **eject the strand** and free the pore. Enrichment without any wet-lab capture step.

## Deep sequencing

::: {.incremental}
- **Ultra-deep sequencing** — coverage of 50×, 100×, or even 500–1000×.
- Also called **high-sensitivity sequencing**.
- Used when high-quality sequence is required, or when the target DNA or RNA occurs at **very low frequency** relative to everything else in the sample.
- The purpose is to identify **rare genetic variation** — somatic variants, minority pathogen strains, low-frequency alleles in a pool.
:::

# Molecular ecology applications

## Time of the 'omics

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p43_2.jpg){height="400px"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p43_3.jpg){height="400px"}
:::
:::

DNA, RNA, proteins, metabolites — potential, expression, and activity, each with its own sequencing-based readout.

## Time of 'big data'

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p44_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p21_2.jpg)

The bottleneck moved from the bench to the pipeline: QC, assembly, annotation, taxonomic and functional profiling, and validation — each a set of choices that change the answer.
:::
:::

## Marker discovery and genotyping

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p45_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- **SNPs**;
- **Restriction-site associated DNA (RAD) sequencing**;
- **microsatellite discovery** and genotyping.

RADseq is Lecture 2's RFLP logic with a sequencer at the end: digest, size-select, sequence around the cut sites, call SNPs at thousands of loci.
:::
:::

## Single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p46_3.jpg)

![](/assets/lecture3/p46_2.jpg){height="200px"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
A **SNP** is a substitution of a single nucleotide at a specific position in the genome that is present in a **sufficiently large fraction of the population — 1% or more**. Rarer than that, and we call it a **mutation**.

SNPs fall in noncoding or coding regions; coding SNPs are **synonymous** or **non-synonymous**, and non-synonymous ones **missense** or **nonsense**.
:::
:::

## Transcriptomics

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p47_2.jpg){height="400px"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
- The **transcriptome** is the population of RNA molecules; **transcriptomics** is its functional characterisation.
- **2007–2017**: 575 ecological studies used microarrays or **RNA-seq**.
- **Reverse transcriptase**: RNA → cDNA.
- **SAGE** — serial analysis of gene expression — analyses the frequency of genes in a cDNA library.
- **Gene expression profiling** characterises which genes are expressed in a tissue *and at what level*.
- **Candidate gene finding** — identifying the genes or regulatory sequences underlying a trait or behaviour.
:::
:::

## Single-cell resolution

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p47_3.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](/assets/lecture3/p47_4.jpg){height="90px"}

Barcoded gel beads in droplets give every cell its own barcode, so one library holds the transcriptional profile of thousands of **individual cells** rather than their average.
:::
:::

## Epigenomics

::: {.incremental}
- **Epigenetics** is the study of changes in gene expression caused by modifications to the bases in a DNA sequence, rather than by differences in the sequence itself.
- The common modification is addition of a **methyl group** to cytosine or adenine.
- Methylation patterns differ between species and alter gene expression.
- Other modifications include **post-translational modification of histones**, which remodels chromatin and alters transcription.
- **Transgenerational effects** — conditions experienced by the parental generation influence the offspring generation.
:::

## Epigenomics — the methods

::: {.incremental}
- **MSAP** — methylation-sensitive amplification polymorphism: two or more endonuclease **isoschizomers** that recognise the same site but differ in sensitivity to methylation.
- **Methylation sequencing** brings NGS throughput and genome-wide analysis while resolving methylation at the **single-nucleotide level**.
- **WGBS** — whole-genome bisulphite sequencing: sodium bisulphite converts non-methylated cytosines to uracil (read as thymine), while **methylated cytosines are protected**.
- **ChIP-seq** — chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing: studies post-translational modification of histone proteins, particularly methylation and acetylation of N-terminal tail residues.
:::

## Platform characteristics — long read

![](/assets/lecture3/p51_3.jpg){height="450px"}

## Check yourself

<details>
<summary>What separates second- from third-generation sequencing?</summary>

Amplification. Second-generation platforms need clonal copies of each fragment to produce enough signal; third-generation platforms read a single molecule, which removes amplification bias and allows very long reads.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why did 454 struggle with homopolymers?</summary>

The light signal is proportional to the number of identical bases incorporated in one flow, so a run of, say, seven A's has to be distinguished from six or eight by intensity alone.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Q30 means what, exactly?</summary>

A 1 in 1000 probability that the base call is wrong — 99.9% accuracy. Q = −10·log₁₀(P_error).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why combine short and long reads for a genome assembly?</summary>

Long reads span repeats and structural variants so contigs join up; short reads have far lower per-base error, so they polish the consensus. Neither alone gives a contiguous *and* accurate assembly.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why does bisulphite treatment let you read methylation?</summary>

Unmethylated cytosines are deaminated to uracil and then read as thymine, while methylated cytosines are protected and still read as C. Every C remaining in the read was methylated.

</details>
